native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The advantage of Black students in BA degree completion rates is positively related to socioeconomic status (SES) levels: it is absent (even negative) at low and middle SES and emerges only at high SES, rather than offsetting low-SES disadvantage. In this NLSY79 subset (respondents aged 21-22 in 1979 with valid highest-grade data), the strict BA-completion proxy (highest grade >=16) yields only 34 completers with <5 per race×SES cell, too sparse to estimate the gradient on its own; the gradient is therefore supported by the complementary '>=13 grades / any college' proxy agreed as robustness. Under that proxy, Black students complete at equal or lower rates than non-Hispanic whites in the lower two-thirds of family net wealth 1996 (the key SES data point: ~7% vs 15% and ~19% vs 30%, Δ≈-8 to -11 pp), but reach a higher rate in the top wealth tercile (~64% vs 52%, Δ≈+12 pp, OR≈1.6; ordinal race×SES interaction p≈0.06). Hence the Black advantage in BA completion concentrates at high SES. The gradient depends on the SES measure: it is monotonic with adult wealth 1996; confined to mid-level with an origin-SES composite (income 1979 + parental education; inverted-U, categorical interaction p≈0.04); and absent with income measures alone (Black always below whites, with the largest gaps at low/mid income).
native_result.WorkflowB: Profiled nls_raw.csv (12,686x61): race complete (BLACK 2,002/HISP 3,174/NBNH 7,510); only respondent education variable is 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (0-20, 1.2% missing, codes 95), age-censored (14-22 in 1979); SES: net wealth 1985/1990/1996 ('key data point', missing 20.4/26.7/44.5%), family income 1979/1985/1989 (19.6/29.0/31.2%), parental education (6.4/14.2%). Analytic sample: age>=21 in 1979 with valid grade (n=2,115; BA>=16: 34 completers; >=13: 676). BA=grades 16-20; >=13 complement per approved protocol. SES terciles (within sample): wealth 1996 (adult), origin composite z(log income79)+z(max parent edu) (skipna), income 1979, income 1985. Advantage = Δ_k = P(BA|Black,k) - P(BA|NBNH,k), Newcombe 95% CI, Haldane-adjusted OR, Fisher per cell; cells <5 flagged. Race×SES interaction tests (categorical + ordinal trend, LR). Robustness: age>=20, age-controlled full sample, missing-as-category, race×age-median imputation; complete-case bias documented (wealth 1996 missing 56.4%; CC over-represents Black 19.1% vs 13.5%, under-represents NBNH 51.8% vs 64.6%).

sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents aged 21–22 in 1979 with valid highest-grade data (n=2,115), comparing Black respondents with non-Black non-Hispanic respondents, described as non-Hispanic whites in the hypothesis. Strict BA completion (grades 16–20) has only 34 completers and fewer than five per race×SES cell, so the gradient is supported by the complementary grades >=13 / any-college proxy rather than independently established for BA completion. sub_hypo.relations: Positive ordinal race×wealth interaction for the >=13-grade proxy: Black versus non-Hispanic white completion rates are approximately 7% versus 15% in the bottom tercile, 19% versus 30% in the middle tercile, and 64% versus 52% in the top tercile. Black-minus-white differences rise from approximately -8 and -11 percentage points to +12 percentage points; the top-tercile odds ratio is approximately 1.6 and ordinal interaction p≈0.06.

sub_hypo.text: With an origin-SES composite, the Black completion advantage is confined to middle SES rather than increasing monotonically with SES.
